components.text: Challenges whether a Christian salvific purpose can explain suffering among victims belonging to competing faiths.
Challenges whether the proposed salvific purpose applies coherently to victims across competing faiths.
Argues that concrete suffering initially conflicts with the proposed character and purposes of an interested, powerful divine agent.
Uses observable tsunamis and childhood cancers as evidence despite the appeal to inaccessible providential reasons.
Offers suffering as concrete adverse evidence that must enter the total-evidence assessment of divine attributes.
Challenges whether Christian purposes make severe natural suffering unsurprising.
Identifies mystery about unknown greater goods as insufficient because it can insulate virtually any belief from assessment.
Challenges whether limiting what God can actualize coheres with the asserted divine omnipotence.
Challenges the alternative claim that God can prevent suffering but permits it for a greater salvific good.
Challenges whether the free-will limitation and permissive-reason defense jointly preserve divine power and goodness.
Attacks reliance on unknown greater goods as an unrestricted appeal to mystery.
Demands support for the modal claim that God could not create free creatures with comparable good and substantially less suffering.
Demands support for the modal claim that comparable freedom and good require this degree of suffering.
Rejects taking unknown morally sufficient reasons on trust when applied to drowning in a tsunami or dying painfully from cancer.
Challenges the suggestion that severe temporal suffering is somehow ultimately good for the sufferer.
Rejects unknown morally sufficient reasons as inadequate support for trusting that severe suffering is justified.
Defends ordinary comparative moral judgment against paralysis from unknown remote or chaotic consequences.
Defends ordinary comparative moral judgment despite incomplete knowledge of remote causal consequences.
Challenges future compensation as insufficient to reconcile the world's harsh facts with an aware and influential deity.
Adopts the total-scope standard while arguing that the actual world's evidence diminishes the reasonableness of belief.
Challenges future compensation as insufficient to reconcile the harsh world with a caring supernatural agent.
Uses the total scope of evidence to claim that harsh worldly facts diminish reasonableness.
Presses the distinction between a logically possible evil-free free world and its alleged infeasibility for God.
Distinguishes logical possibility of a free natural-evil-free world from its alleged infeasibility for God.
Reframes the recognition of actual evil as support for objective moral values and therefore as part of an affirmative argument for God.
Reframes objective evil from solely adverse evidence into a premise requiring an objective moral foundation.
Accepts that some acts are genuinely wrong while shifting the dispute to their ontological foundation.
Supplies an alternative grounding for moral demands in objective facts about sentience, human needs, interests, and vulnerability to suffering.
Offers objective human needs, interests, sentience, and suffering as a secular basis for moral demands.
Diagnoses the human-needs foundation as species-relative because differently evolved rational creatures could endorse incompatible values.
Argues that evolved human needs and attitudes remain species-relative rather than objectively authoritative.
Argues that the actual facts of another person's pain constrain choice even after acknowledging humanity's animal and evolutionary status.
Offers suffering-based moral reasons as an alternative to grounding obligation in God.
Argues that facts about another's suffering constrain action despite the evolutionary contingency objection.
Provides a nondivine experiential basis for respect and kindness.
Offers a specified class of providential reasons: coordinating disasters and wars toward freely bringing more people into relationship with God.
Connects natural disasters to a universal maximizing aim of freely bringing people into divine relationship.
Supplies a kingdom-building purpose rather than relying solely on future compensation.
Supplies a proposed providential structure in which disasters may contribute to freely formed relationship with God.
Invokes a wider kingdom-building purpose rather than compensation alone.
Offers a benevolent-purpose alternative to the initial adverse attribute inference.
Answers that God cannot causally guarantee right choices while preserving significant freedom, so comparable moral good without moral evil may be unavailable.
Provides a feasibility constraint based on the counterfactual conduct of genuinely free moral agents.
Answers that God cannot causally guarantee right choices while preserving significant creaturely freedom.
Offers a modal reason why an evil-free free world might not be feasible for God.
Denies that the observed evils establish either logical incompatibility or a warranted confident probabilistic rejection of Christian theism.
Reasserts a possible theistic explanation as sufficient to answer the strict logical incompatibility claim.
Reasserts epistemic limits against confident probability judgments from apparently gratuitous suffering.
Returns the dispute to Christian purposes and the wider evidential context.
Challenges extension of ordinary judgments into confident assessments of divine providential probabilities.
Answers the adverse inference by combining logical compatibility, epistemic limits, Christian purposes, and wider evidence.
Reasserts a possible free-will explanation establishing compatibility.
Reasserts limits on confident probability judgments about divine reasons.
Places suffering within Christian doctrine and the total evidential context.
